newsitem.title: USA: Bill Cosby extortion case goes to jury.
newsitem.headline: Bill Cosby extortion case goes to jury.

text.p: The federal jury deciding whether a young woman tried to extort $40 million from entertainer Bill Cosby was instructed on Wednesday that it is irrelevant whether the actor is the defendant's real father.

The jury of seven men and five women began deliberations shortly before noon in the case against Autumn Jackson, 22, who claims to be Cosby's illegitimate daughter. Deliberations ended late in the afternoon and will resume on Thursday.

Jackson, along with Jose Medina, 51, and Boris Sabas, also known as Boris Shmulevich, 42, are on trial for threatening to ruin Cosby's reputation by selling Jackson's story to a supermarket tabloid newpaper.

They are charged with conspiracy, extortion and violating the federal law that prohibits the use of interstate commerce to commit crimes. If convicted of all counts, they face a possible total prison term of 12 years and fines of $750,000.

Among evidence that the jury has asked to review is testimony by Placido Macaraeg, who had worked with Jackson and Medina on a failed children's television show last year. Macaraeg testified about efforts by Medina and Jackson to pressure Cosby to pay the $40 million.
He quoted Medina as saying, "If he (Cosby) doesn't want this to get out, he's going to have to pay a lot of money."

U.S. District Judge Barbara Jones instructed jurors on the law they must follow before reaching a verdict. She warned them against being swayed by sympathy and told them that whether Cosby is actually Jackson's father is not a defence.
"It is irrelevant whether Bill Cosby is the father of Autumn Jackson," Jones said.
She also said it was irrelevant whether the defendant was owed money.

The key issue was whether the defendants conspired to extort money from Cosby by threatening to ruin the actor's reputation. She said the law forbids anyone trying to obtain a victim's property by threatening to take actions that would subject the person to "hatred, contempt or ridicule."
However, Jones said that if the government had not proven that Jackson had an intent to commit extortion, jurors could not find her guilty of that crime.

Jackson's defence lawyer has argued that Jackson believed she is Cosby's daughter and that she was engaged in legitimate negotiations to money that was rightfully hers. He said she did not think she was breaking the law.

During the trial, prosecutors had introduced as evidence recorded telephone conversations and letters in which Jackson contacted Cosby's lawyer, his publisher, CBS and Cosby's television sponsors and threatened to expose the actor as a deadbeat dad unless she received money.
As part of the scheme, Jackson sent Cosby's lawyer and the former president of CBS an unsigned contract with the Globe supermarket tabloid for the sale of her story for $25,000.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul Englemayer said the fact that the contract was unsigned made it a threat with the message "I'm one signature away from ruining your reputation."
